iconicAnchor.label: Papel picado in Día de los Muertos observance
iconicAnchor.creatorOrTradition: Mexican and Mexican American cut-paper traditions
iconicAnchor.whyCanonical: The National Museum of the American Latino describes papel picado as chiseled stacks of tissue paper and places it within a specific community celebration rather than generic party decoration.

sources.title: DC Day of the Dead / Día de los Muertos
sources.publisher: National Museum of the American Latino
supports: Papel picado is made by chiseling stacked tissue paper to create cut or perforated designs within a living festival context.

sources.title: 5 Facts About Día de los Muertos
supports: Traditional papel picado banners are contextual symbols within Día de los Muertos and can represent wind on an ofrenda.

culturalContext.note: Identify the exact festival, community, material, and function. Papel picado, procession banners, prayer flags, and other suspended forms are distinct practices, some devotional or memorial. Do not mix their symbols, invent sacred text, or strip them into generic party decoration; collaborate with makers for direct contemporary use.
